To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the vertical zonation patterns of non-host animals in a soft-bottom intertidals system are influenced by the presence of a parasite of the dominant host species.
the vertical zonation patterns of four non-host animals in a soft-bottom intertidaldomain are influenced by the zonation of a host species that is heavily parasitized.
“Parasitism of the bivalve Austrovenus by echinostomes influences the zonation of other organisms by changing the availability and quality of cockle substrates.”
In summary, our research is concerned with
how parasites can affect the vertical zonation patterns of organisms in intertidal habitats, and the implications of this for the structure and functioning of communities in these environments.
the effects of parasites on host behaviour and the consequences of this for the distribution of non-host species.
how parasitism can influence community structure and the zonation of organisms in intertidal habitats.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
parasites have the potential to influence the zonation and distribution of many species and that their impact on zonational patterns may be substantial.
parasitism can influence zonation of organisms, and that it can do so both indirectly, via effects on the host, and directly, by altering the distribution of the parasite itself.
the parasite is the primary factor influencing the vertical zonation pattern of the four species in this study, and that the parasite is a keystone species in the community.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the zonation of the cockle A. stutchburyi is determined by the balance of the effects of the physical environment and predation, whereas the zonation of its parasites is determined by the cockle, and the zonation of other animals is determined by the effects of both the cockle and its parasites.
parasites can influence the vertical zonation patterns of animals by influencing the zonation of their hosts.
parasites have the potential to influence the zonation, and hence the community structure, of organisms in soft-sediment intertidal habitats.
The main takeaway from our work is that
parasites should be considered as a potential factor in the zonation of organisms in intertidal habitats.
parasitism can be a major factor influencing the vertical zonation patterns of organisms in soft-sediment habitats.
parasitism is not only important in structuring communities but also in determining how communities are organized vertically in space.
